steps: Step 1, Stretch a rubber band over an open box and pluck it. You see it vibrate and hear a sound. Touch it lightly and the sound stops. Conclusion: sound is made when objects vibrate.

Step 2, Test pitch. Pluck a short band and a long band of the same thickness stretched over the box. The shorter, tighter band vibrates faster and gives a higher pitch. Pitch depends on how fast the vibration is: more vibrations per second means higher pitch.

Step 3, Test loudness. Hit a drum softly, then hard. The harder hit makes a bigger vibration and a louder sound. Loudness depends on the size of the vibration, measured in decibels, and has no link to pitch.

Step 4, Test travel. Tie a string between two paper cups and pull it tight. Speak into one cup while a friend listens to the other 5 m away. Sound travels along the string. It also travels through air, water and solids, but not through empty space.

Step 5, Record in a table: short band, high pitch, soft; long band, low pitch, soft; drum hit hard, loud. Conclusion: vibration makes sound, speed of vibration sets pitch, and size of vibration sets loudness.
Step 6, Your turn: a guitar string is made shorter by pressing it. Is the pitch higher or lower? Answer: higher, because a shorter string vibrates faster.
Step 1, Build a series circuit with two 1.5 V cells in a row (3 V total), two bulbs and a switch. Both bulbs glow equally. Unscrew one bulb and the other goes out because the loop is broken.

Step 2, Build a parallel circuit with the same cells, giving each bulb its own branch. Both glow brighter than in series. Unscrew one bulb and the other stays lit, which is why house lights are wired in parallel.

Step 3, Make an electromagnet. Wind 30 turns of insulated wire around an iron nail and connect it through a switch to two 1.5 V cells. It may pick up about 6 paper clips; 60 turns picks up more. Switch off when not testing, as the wire warms.

Step 4, Test a bar magnet on a tray of objects. It attracts iron nails, steel pins and steel paper clips but not plastic, wood, copper or aluminium foil. Two north poles repel; a north and south pole attract.
Step 5, Uses: electromagnets lift scrap metal in a yard and ring doorbells, and compasses use magnets to point north. A switch in the circuit turns an electromagnet off to drop its load.

Step 6, Your turn: if the nail picks up 6 clips with 30 turns, how many clips would you predict with 90 turns, and why? Answer: roughly 18, because more turns make a stronger field, assuming the same supply.

Step 1, Test a bar magnet on 7 items. It picks up a nail, a paper clip and a steel pin but not an aluminium can, plastic comb, copper coin or rubber. Magnets attract magnetic materials: iron, steel, nickel and cobalt.

Step 2, Find poles. Dip the bar in iron filings: most cling to the two ends, which are the poles. Hang the bar by a thread; it settles pointing north-south. The end pointing north is the north-seeking pole.
Step 3, Test attraction and repulsion. Bring two north poles together and they push apart. Bring north to south and they pull together. Like poles repel, unlike poles attract.

Step 4, Test air. Invert a glass over a floating cork in water; the water level inside stays lower, so air takes up space. Squeeze a closed balloon to show air can be compressed. Air also has about 21 per cent oxygen, which we need for breathing and burning.
Step 5, Test water. Measure 100 mL of water in a tall and a wide glass: the same volume takes different shapes. Water dissolves salt and sugar and is needed for all life.
Step 6, Your turn: which items in a pile of a rubber, a steel spoon, a coin of copper and an iron screw will a magnet lift? Answer: the steel spoon and the iron screw.
Step 1, Test ice. Melt an ice cube in a cup at 25 C: it becomes water, the same substance, and can freeze again. This is a physical change, reversible, with no new substance formed.
Step 2, Burn a small piece of paper in a safe metal tray with adult help. It becomes ash and smoke and cannot return to paper. A new substance formed, so this is a chemical change.

Step 3, Add 1 teaspoon of baking soda to 50 mL of vinegar in a bottle. It fizzes and gives carbon dioxide gas. Bubbles and a new gas show a chemical change. Test by lowering a lit splinter: it goes out.

Step 4, Make a table with signs of chemical change: new colour, gas, heat or light, precipitate, new smell. Compare with physical changes: shape, size, state, no new substance. Dissolving salt in water is physical because evaporation brings the salt back.
Step 5, Classify: rusting of iron chemical, curdling of milk chemical, cutting a vegetable physical, boiling water physical, cooking an egg chemical, folding paper physical.
Step 6, Your turn: classify a rotting banana and crushing a can. Answer: rotting is chemical (new substances, smell, colour); crushing is physical (shape changes only).

Step 1, Test a leaf for starch with adult help. Take a leaf from a plant kept in sun for 6 hours. Boil it in water, then soften it in alcohol heated only in a hot water bath, never a flame. Rinse, add iodine: blue-black shows starch.

Step 2, Write the equation in words: carbon dioxide + water, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, gives glucose + oxygen. Say where each enters: CO2 through stomata, water from roots, light absorbed by chlorophyll in chloroplasts.

Step 3, Control the test. A leaf covered with black paper for the same time stays brown with iodine, showing no starch. This proves light is needed. A variegated leaf stains only in its green part, proving chlorophyll is needed.

Step 4, Follow digestion of a cheese sandwich. Mouth: teeth chew and amylase in saliva starts breaking starch into sugar. Stomach: acid and pepsin digest protein. Small intestine: bile and enzymes finish digestion, and absorption goes into blood through villi.

Step 5, Trace the path: mouth, food pipe, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum. The small intestine is about 6 m long in an adult, giving a large surface for absorption. The large intestine absorbs water.
Step 6, Your turn: name the gas given off in photosynthesis and the organ where most absorption occurs. Answer: oxygen; the small intestine.

Step 1, Compare materials. Cotton and wool are natural fibres from plants and animals. Nylon, polyester and acrylic are synthetic fibres made from petrochemicals. Nylon is strong and light, so it is used in ropes and parachutes.

Step 2, Teacher demonstration only, outdoors or in a ventilated space, with tongs on tiny samples; never at home. Cotton burns with a paper smell and ash. Wool smells like burning hair. Nylon melts into a bead and shrinks from the flame, showing a synthetic.
Step 3, Compare in a table: absorbs water (cotton yes, polyester little), dries fast (polyester yes), strength (nylon high), cost and durability. Wash a 10 cm swatch of each and note wet weights.

Step 4, Explain plastics. They are polymers, long chains of repeating units. Thermoplastics like polythene soften on heating and can be remoulded. Thermosetting plastics like bakelite harden permanently and are used for electrical switches.

Step 5, Discuss environment: plastic is non-biodegradable and can last hundreds of years. Use the 5 R principle: reduce, reuse, recycle, recover and refuse. Sort plastics by recycling code and send to proper collection.

Step 6, Your turn: which fibre would you choose for a raincoat and which for summer wear, and why? Answer: a synthetic like nylon or polyester that repels water for the raincoat; cotton for summer as it absorbs sweat.

Step 1, Test properties of samples: iron, copper, aluminium, sulphur, carbon, and zinc. Metals are shiny, hard, malleable (hammer into sheets), ductile (draw into wire) and sonorous when struck. Sulphur is dull and brittle.

Step 2, Test conductivity with a 3 V circuit. Copper, aluminium and iron light the bulb. Sulphur does not. Graphite, a form of carbon, is a non-metal that conducts. Record exceptions: mercury is a liquid metal, graphite conducts.

Step 3, Teacher demonstration of reactions with oxygen; wear goggles. Burn magnesium ribbon with tongs, without looking straight at the bright white flame. It forms white magnesium oxide, which turns red litmus blue, so it is basic. Sulphur burns in a fume cupboard only; its oxide gives an acid.
Step 4, Write the equation: 2Mg + O2 gives 2MgO. Check atoms: 2 Mg and 2 O on each side. Conclusion: metal oxides are generally basic, non-metal oxides are generally acidic.

Step 5, Link uses to properties: copper for wires (ductile, conductor), aluminium foil for packing (malleable), iron for bridges (strong), sulphur for gunpowder and matches, carbon as graphite in pencils and as fuel.
Step 6, Your turn: a silvery solid hammers into a sheet and rings when struck. Is it a metal? Name its oxide's nature. Answer: yes, a metal; its oxide is likely basic.

Step 1, Build a food chain. Grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, eagle. Name the producer (grass), primary consumer (grasshopper), secondary consumer (frog), tertiary consumer (snake) and quaternary, top consumer (eagle). Add decomposers like bacteria.
Step 2, Apply the 10 per cent law. If grass captures 10,000 J, the grasshopper gets 1000 J, the frog 100 J, the snake 10 J and the eagle 1 J. Hence food chains are short, usually 3 to 5 levels.

Step 3, Analyse waste. Biodegradable waste like vegetable peels is broken down by microbes. Non-biodegradable waste like plastic stays. Biomagnification: a pesticide at 0.02 ppm in water can reach much higher levels in top predators.
Step 4, Discuss the ozone layer. UV breaks O2 and O3 in the stratosphere. Chlorofluorocarbons release chlorine atoms which destroy ozone, so their use was curbed. Ozone absorbs harmful UV.

Step 5, Plan resource use. Use the 3 Rs, rainwater harvesting, and water management. Compare coal and petroleum as non-renewable fossil fuels with solar and wind as renewable. Use CNG to cut air pollution.
Step 6, Your turn: a producer fixes 5000 J. How much reaches the tertiary consumer by the 10 per cent law? Answer: 5000 to 500 to 50 to 5 J, so 5 J.
Step 1, Describe SHM x = A sin(omega t) with A = 0.05 m and period T = 2 s. omega = 2 pi / T = 3.14 rad/s. Maximum speed = A omega = 0.157 m/s and maximum acceleration = A omega^2 = 0.49 m/s2.
Step 2, Spring-mass system. m = 0.5 kg and k = 200 N/m. T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k) = 2 pi sqrt(0.0025) = 2 pi x 0.05 = 0.314 s, so f = 3.18 Hz.
Step 3, Simple pendulum. L = 1 m gives T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g) = 2 pi sqrt(1/9.8) = 2.01 s. Quadrupling L to 4 m doubles T to 4.01 s.
Step 4, Energy in SHM. For the spring system with A = 0.1 m: total energy = 0.5 k A^2 = 0.5 x 200 x 0.01 = 1 J. At x = 0.05 m, PE = 0.5 x 200 x 0.0025 = 0.25 J, so KE = 0.75 J.

Step 5, Wave speed v = f lambda. A wave of f = 50 Hz and lambda = 6.8 m travels at 340 m/s. On a string, v = sqrt(T/mu): with T = 100 N and mu = 0.01 kg/m, v = 100 m/s. Fundamental on 1 m string: f = v / 2L = 50 Hz.
Step 6, Your turn: find the period of a 0.25 m pendulum (g = 9.8). Answer: 2 pi sqrt(0.25/9.8) = 1.00 s.
Step 1, Calculate molality. 18 g of glucose (180 g/mol) is 0.1 mol, dissolved in 500 g of water. m = 0.1 / 0.5 = 0.2 mol/kg. Mole fraction of glucose = 0.1 / (0.1 + 27.8) = 0.0036.

Step 2, Find the boiling point elevation. delta Tb = Kb m = 0.52 x 0.2 = 0.104 K, so the solution boils at 100.104 C. Freezing point depression with Kf = 1.86: delta Tf = 0.372 K, freezing at -0.372 C.
Step 3, Calculate molar mass from osmotic pressure. A solution of 2 g solute in 1 L gives pi = 0.0246 atm at 300 K. M = wRT / (pi V) = 2 x 0.0821 x 300 / 0.0246 = 2002 g/mol, a polymer-like value.

Step 4, Apply the van't Hoff factor. 0.1 m NaCl has i near 2, so delta Tf = 2 x 1.86 x 0.1 = 0.372 K, twice that of glucose at 0.1 m. Relative lowering of vapour pressure equals the solute mole fraction.

Step 5, Calculate a cell potential. Zn + Cu2+ gives Zn2+ + Cu. E cell = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10 V. Nernst at 298 K: E = 1.10 - (0.0592/2) log([Zn2+]/[Cu2+]). With [Zn2+] = 0.01 and [Cu2+] = 1, E = 1.10 + 0.0592 = 1.159 V.
Step 6, Your turn: find delta Tf for 0.5 m glucose in water (Kf = 1.86). Answer: 1.86 x 0.5 = 0.93 K, so freezing at -0.93 C.
Step 1, Describe the nucleus. Carbon-14 has Z = 6 and A = 14, so 8 neutrons. Nuclear radius R = R0 A^(1/3) with R0 = 1.2 fm gives R = 1.2 x 14^(1/3) = 2.89 fm. Density is about 2.3 x 10^17 kg/m3.

Step 2, Calculate binding energy using atomic masses. Helium-4 has mass 4.0026 u against 2 hydrogen atoms (1.00783 u) and 2 neutrons (1.00866 u) summing to 4.03298 u. Mass defect 0.0304 u x 931.5 MeV/u = 28.3 MeV, so about 7.1 MeV per nucleon.
Step 3, Radioactive decay. N = N0 (1/2)^(t/T). A sample with half-life 5 days is 800 mg. After 15 days, N = 800 / 8 = 100 mg. Decay constant lambda = 0.693 / T = 0.139 per day.

Step 4, Write nuclear reactions. Alpha decay: U-238 gives Th-234 + He-4. Beta decay: C-14 gives N-14 + electron + antineutrino. Fission: U-235 + n gives Ba-141 + Kr-92 + 3n + about 200 MeV. Fusion: 4 H gives He.

Step 5, Semiconductors. A p-n junction diode conducts in forward bias; in reverse bias there is a small leakage. A half-wave rectifier passes one half cycle. Silicon has a band gap of 1.1 eV. N-type doping with phosphorus; p-type with boron.
Step 6, Your turn: a 400 mg sample has half-life 2 h. How much remains after 6 h? Answer: 400 / 8 = 50 mg.
